expectedText:
CCPA SERVICE PROVIDER DATA PROCESSING AGREEMENT
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · DataProcessing Solutions LLC

RECITALS AND BUSINESS PURPOSE
This CCPA Service Provider Data Processing Agreement ("Agreement") is entered into between Acme, Inc. ("Business") and DataProcessing Solutions LLC ("Service Provider"). Business discloses personal information to Service Provider so that Service Provider can process it on Business's behalf for the following business purpose: processing customer support tickets and providing technical support services. This Agreement sets out the terms Business and Service Provider intend to satisfy the requirements described in California Civil Code §§ 1798.100(d) and 1798.140(ag) for disclosures of personal information to a service provider under the California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act.

"BUSINESS" AND "SERVICE PROVIDER" ARE DEFINED TERMS
California's Consumer Privacy Act uses "business" and "service provider" as specific, defined terms — not every company that hires a vendor is a "business" under this statute, and not every vendor is a "service provider" under it. A "business" is a for-profit entity that does business in California, collects or directs the collection of consumers' personal information, and meets at least one of three thresholds: annual gross revenue above $25,000,000, annually buying, selling, or sharing the personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households, or deriving 50% or more of annual revenue from selling or sharing personal information. A "service provider" is a person that processes personal information on Acme, Inc.'s behalf and receives it for a business purpose under a written contract that meets specific statutory conditions described elsewhere in this document. Whether Acme, Inc. meets the statutory revenue or volume thresholds, and whether DataProcessing Solutions LLC's processing arrangement meets the statutory conditions for "service provider" status, are factual questions this document does not resolve.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Business” means:(1) A sole proprietorship, partnership, limited liability company, corporation, association, or other legal entity that is organized or operated for the profit or financial benefit of its shareholders or other owners, that collects consumers’ personal information, or on the behalf of which such information is collected and that alone, or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of consumers’ personal information, that does business in the State of California, and that satisfies one or more of the following thresholds:(A) As of January 1 of the calendar year, had annual gross revenues in excess of twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000) in the preceding calendar year, as adjusted pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 1798.199.95.(B) Alone or in combination, annually buys, sells, or shares the personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households.(C) Derives 50 percent or more of its annual revenues from selling or sharing consumers’ personal information."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of "business" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.140.)
  "“Service provider” means a person that processes personal information on behalf of a business and that receives from or on behalf of the business consumer’s personal information for a business purpose pursuant to a written contract, provided that the contract prohibits the person from:(A) Selling or sharing the personal information.(B) Retaining, using, or disclosing the personal information for any purpose other than for the business purposes specified in the contract for the business, including retaining, using, or disclosing the personal information for a commercial purpose other than the business purposes specified in the contract with the business, or as otherwise permitted by this title.(C) Retaining, using, or disclosing the information outside of the direct business relationship between the service provider and the business.(D) Combining the personal information that the service provider receives from, or on behalf of, the business with personal information that it receives from, or on behalf of, another person or persons, or collects from its own interaction with the consumer, provided that the service provider may combine personal information to perform any business purpose as defined in regulations adopted pursuant to paragraph (9) of subdivision (a) of Section 1798.185, except as provided for in paragraph (6) of subdivision (e) of this section and in regulations adopted by the California Privacy Protection Agency."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of "service provider" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.140.)
  Known gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statute, Civil Code § 1798.140 — subdivision (d)(1) ("business") and subdivision (ag)(1) ("service provider") — because both definitions come from the same statutory definitions section and are necessary to explain who this document's two defined roles correspond to. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Consumer Privacy Act (as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act) — not a claim about which state's law governs this document or any party's obligations under it. This document addresses only California's CCPA/CPRA framework; it does not address the EU/UK GDPR, other states' privacy statutes (e.g., Virginia, Colorado, Connecticut, Utah, or the many other state privacy laws now in force), or any other jurisdiction's data-processing requirements, which use different definitions and impose different or additional contract terms. The "business" definition's full text also includes an alternate "controlled entity" category (§ 1798.140(d)(2)), a joint-venture category (§ 1798.140(d)(3)), and a voluntary-certification category (§ 1798.140(d)(4)) not quoted here because they describe corporate-structure edge cases outside this document's two-party scope. No case law interpreting these definitions was checked; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

TWO SEPARATE STATUTORY SOURCES OF REQUIRED CONTRACT TERMS
The CCPA imposes required contract terms in two separate places, not one, and a compliant agreement needs to satisfy both. First, Civil Code § 1798.140(ag)(1) makes these terms part of the definition of "service provider" itself: a written contract only creates "service provider" status if it prohibits the recipient from (A) selling or sharing the personal information; (B) retaining, using, or disclosing the personal information for any purpose other than the business purposes specified in the contract; (C) retaining, using, or disclosing the information outside the direct business relationship between the recipient and the business; and (D) combining the personal information with personal information the recipient receives from other sources, except as separately permitted by regulation. Second, and independently, Civil Code § 1798.100(d) imposes a general duty on any business that discloses personal information to a service provider or contractor for a business purpose: the business "shall enter into an agreement" that (1) specifies the information is disclosed only for limited and specified purposes; (2) obligates the recipient to comply with the CCPA and to provide the same level of privacy protection the statute requires; (3) grants the business rights to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure the recipient's compliant use of the information; (4) requires the recipient to notify the business if it determines it can no longer meet its CCPA obligations; and (5) grants the business the right, on notice, to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate unauthorized use.

Correction to this document's working assumption: the task brief that prompted this research treated § 1798.100(d) and § 1798.140(ag) as alternative possible locations for the required contract terms ("§ 1798.100(d) or § 1798.140(ag) or similar"). Checking the actual statutory text shows they are not alternatives — both provisions impose real, independent, and only partly overlapping contract-term requirements, and this document's operative contract-terms clause is drafted to satisfy both lists rather than treating either one as sufficient by itself. WHY A COMPLIANT SERVICE-PROVIDER TRANSFER IS NOT A "SALE" OR "SHARE"
The CCPA defines "sell" as disclosing a consumer's personal information "to a third party for monetary or other valuable consideration," and defines "share" as disclosing personal information "to a third party for cross-context behavioral advertising," whether or not for consideration. Both definitions depend on the recipient being a "third party." The statute's definition of "third party" expressly excludes two categories of recipient: "(2) A service provider to the business," and "(3) A contractor." Read together, these three definitions are the statutory mechanism this document relies on: a disclosure of personal information to a recipient who meets the statutory definition of "service provider" is, by the statute's own definitional structure, not a disclosure "to a third party" at all — and because both "sell" and "share" are defined only as disclosures to a third party, such a disclosure falls outside both definitions.

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ad)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of "sell" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.140.)

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ai) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of "third party" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1798.140.)

AUDIT RIGHTS ARE PERMISSIVE, NOT A STATUTORY MANDATE
The CCPA does not require every service-provider contract to include an audit clause. Civil Code § 1798.140(ag)(1) states that the contract "may, subject to agreement with the service provider, permit the business to monitor the service provider's compliance with the contract through measures, including, but not limited to, ongoing manual reviews and automated scans and regular assessments, audits, or other technical and operational testing at least once every 12 months" — permissive language ("may... permit"), conditioned on the service provider's own agreement, that sets a minimum once-per-12-months cadence only if an audit mechanism is included at all. Separately, Civil Code § 1798.100(d)(3) and (d)(5) do impose a mandatory (not optional) requirement that the business's agreement with the service provider grant the business "rights to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure" the service provider's compliant use of the information, and the right, on notice, "to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate unauthorized use." That mandatory language requires some mechanism for the business to police compliance, but its own text does not specify that the mechanism must be an audit right, on-site inspection, or any particular verification procedure.

WHAT FOLLOWS, UNDER THE STATUTE'S OWN DEFINITIONS, IF THE CONTRACT TERMS ARE MISSING
The statute's definitions are structured so that a written contract lacking the terms described in Civil Code § 1798.140(ag)(1)(A)-(D) has a specific definitional consequence. "Service provider" status under § 1798.140(ag)(1) exists only "provided that the contract prohibits the person from" the four listed things. A recipient processing personal information under a contract that does not meet that condition does not fall within the statutory definition of "service provider." Because § 1798.140(ai) defines "third party" as a person who is not a service provider or a contractor, a recipient who is not a "service provider" and not a "contractor" falls within the definition of "third party" instead. And because "sell" (§ 1798.140(ad)(1)) and "share" (§ 1798.140(ah)(1)) are both defined as disclosures of personal information "to a third party" — for consideration in the case of a sale, for cross-context behavioral advertising in the case of a share — a disclosure to a recipient who is a "third party" for lack of a compliant contract can fall within the statutory definition of a sale or a share of personal information, depending on the nature of the disclosure and the consideration or purpose involved.

SERVICE PROVIDER'S RESTRICTIONS ON USE OF PERSONAL INFORMATION
In processing personal information that Acme, Inc. discloses to it, DataProcessing Solutions LLC shall not: (a) sell or share the personal information; (b) retain, use, or disclose the personal information for any purpose other than the business purpose described in this Agreement (processing customer support tickets and providing technical support services), including for any commercial purpose other than that business purpose, except as otherwise permitted by the California Consumer Privacy Act; (c) retain, use, or disclose the personal information outside the direct business relationship between DataProcessing Solutions LLC and Acme, Inc.; or (d) combine the personal information it receives from Acme, Inc. with personal information it receives from or on behalf of any other person, or collects from its own interaction with the consumer, except as permitted by applicable regulations. DataProcessing Solutions LLC certifies that it understands the restrictions in this clause and will comply with them. If DataProcessing Solutions LLC engages another person to assist in processing personal information for the business purpose described in this Agreement, DataProcessing Solutions LLC shall notify Acme, Inc. of that engagement and shall bind that other person, by written contract, to observe the same restrictions set out in this clause. Acme, Inc. may take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure that DataProcessing Solutions LLC uses the personal information consistently with this Agreement, including through periodic assessments, audits, or other technical and operational testing, and DataProcessing Solutions LLC shall notify Acme, Inc. if it determines that it can no longer meet the restrictions in this clause.

Second, and independently, Civil Code § 1798.100(d) imposes a general duty on any business that discloses personal information to a service provider or contractor for a business purpose: the business "shall enter into an agreement" that (1) specifies the information is disclosed only for limited and specified purposes; (2) obligates the recipient to comply with the CCPA and to provide the same level of privacy protection the statute requires; (3) grants the business rights to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure the recipient's compliant use of the information; (4) requires the recipient to notify the business if it determines it can no longer meet its CCPA obligations; and (5) grants the business the right, on notice, to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate unauthorized use.

citations.quote: provided that the contract prohibits the person from:(A) Selling or sharing the personal information.(B) Retaining, using, or disclosing the personal information for any purpose other than for the business purposes specified in the contract for the business, including retaining, using, or disclosing the personal information for a commercial purpose other than the business purposes specified in the contract with the business, or as otherwise permitted by this title.(C) Retaining, using, or disclosing the information outside of the direct business relationship between the service provider and the business.(D) Combining the personal information that the service provider receives from, or on behalf of, the business with personal information that it receives from, or on behalf of, another person or persons, or collects from its own interaction with the consumer, provided that the service provider may combine personal information to perform any business purpose as defined in regulations adopted pursuant to paragraph (9) of subdivision (a) of Section 1798.185, except as provided for in paragraph (6) of subdivision (e) of this section and in regulations adopted by the California Privacy Protection Agency.

citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, business's general duty to contract with a service provider
citations.quote: A business that collects a consumer’s personal information and that sells that personal information to, or shares it with, a third party or that discloses it to a service provider or contractor for a business purpose shall enter into an agreement with the third party, service provider, or contractor, that:(1) Specifies that the personal information is sold or disclosed by the business only for limited and specified purposes.(2) Obligates the third party, service provider, or contractor to comply with applicable obligations under this title and obligate those persons to provide the same level of privacy protection as is required by this title.(3) Grants the business rights to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure that the third party, service provider, or contractor uses the personal information transferred in a manner consistent with the business’ obligations under this title.(4) Requires the third party, service provider, or contractor to notify the business if it makes a determination that it can no longer meet its obligations under this title.(5) Grants the business the right, upon notice, including under paragraph (4), to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate unauthorized use of personal information.

expectedJSON.body: The CCPA defines "sell" as disclosing a consumer's personal information "to a third party for monetary or other valuable consideration," and defines "share" as disclosing personal information "to a third party for cross-context behavioral advertising," whether or not for consideration. Both definitions depend on the recipient being a "third party." The statute's definition of "third party" expressly excludes two categories of recipient: "(2) A service provider to the business," and "(3) A contractor." Read together, these three definitions are the statutory mechanism this document relies on: a disclosure of personal information to a recipient who meets the statutory definition of "service provider" is, by the statute's own definitional structure, not a disclosure "to a third party" at all — and because both "sell" and "share" are defined only as disclosures to a third party, such a disclosure falls outside both definitions.

citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of "sell"
citations.quote: “Sell,” “selling,” “sale,” or “sold,’’ means selling, renting, releasing, disclosing, disseminating, making available, transferring, or otherwise communicating orally, in writing, or by electronic or other means, a consumer’s personal information by the business to a third party for monetary or other valuable consideration.

citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of "share"
citations.quote: “Share,” “shared,” or “sharing” means sharing, renting, releasing, disclosing, disseminating, making available, transferring, or otherwise communicating orally, in writing, or by electronic or other means, a consumer’s personal information by the business to a third party for cross-context behavioral advertising, whether or not for monetary or other valuable consideration, including transactions between a business and a third party for cross-context behavioral advertising for the benefit of a business in which no money is exchanged.

citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, definition of "third party"
citations.quote: “Third party” means a person who is not any of the following:(1) The business with whom the consumer intentionally interacts and that collects personal information from the consumer as part of the consumer’s current interaction with the business under this title.(2) A service provider to the business.(3) A contractor.

expectedJSON.body: The CCPA does not require every service-provider contract to include an audit clause. Civil Code § 1798.140(ag)(1) states that the contract "may, subject to agreement with the service provider, permit the business to monitor the service provider's compliance with the contract through measures, including, but not limited to, ongoing manual reviews and automated scans and regular assessments, audits, or other technical and operational testing at least once every 12 months" — permissive language ("may... permit"), conditioned on the service provider's own agreement, that sets a minimum once-per-12-months cadence only if an audit mechanism is included at all. Separately, Civil Code § 1798.100(d)(3) and (d)(5) do impose a mandatory (not optional) requirement that the business's agreement with the service provider grant the business "rights to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure" the service provider's compliant use of the information, and the right, on notice, "to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate unauthorized use." That mandatory language requires some mechanism for the business to police compliance, but its own text does not specify that the mechanism must be an audit right, on-site inspection, or any particular verification procedure.

expectedJSON.body: The statute's definitions are structured so that a written contract lacking the terms described in Civil Code § 1798.140(ag)(1)(A)-(D) has a specific definitional consequence. "Service provider" status under § 1798.140(ag)(1) exists only "provided that the contract prohibits the person from" the four listed things. A recipient processing personal information under a contract that does not meet that condition does not fall within the statutory definition of "service provider." Because § 1798.140(ai) defines "third party" as a person who is not a service provider or a contractor, a recipient who is not a "service provider" and not a "contractor" falls within the definition of "third party" instead. And because "sell" (§ 1798.140(ad)(1)) and "share" (§ 1798.140(ah)(1)) are both defined as disclosures of personal information "to a third party" — for consideration in the case of a sale, for cross-context behavioral advertising in the case of a share — a disclosure to a recipient who is a "third party" for lack of a compliant contract can fall within the statutory definition of a sale or a share of personal information, depending on the nature of the disclosure and the consideration or purpose involved.

expectedJSON.body: In processing personal information that Acme, Inc. discloses to it, DataProcessing Solutions LLC shall not: (a) sell or share the personal information; (b) retain, use, or disclose the personal information for any purpose other than the business purpose described in this Agreement (processing customer support tickets and providing technical support services), including for any commercial purpose other than that business purpose, except as otherwise permitted by the California Consumer Privacy Act; (c) retain, use, or disclose the personal information outside the direct business relationship between DataProcessing Solutions LLC and Acme, Inc.; or (d) combine the personal information it receives from Acme, Inc. with personal information it receives from or on behalf of any other person, or collects from its own interaction with the consumer, except as permitted by applicable regulations. DataProcessing Solutions LLC certifies that it understands the restrictions in this clause and will comply with them. If DataProcessing Solutions LLC engages another person to assist in processing personal information for the business purpose described in this Agreement, DataProcessing Solutions LLC shall notify Acme, Inc. of that engagement and shall bind that other person, by written contract, to observe the same restrictions set out in this clause. Acme, Inc. may take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure that DataProcessing Solutions LLC uses the personal information consistently with this Agreement, including through periodic assessments, audits, or other technical and operational testing, and DataProcessing Solutions LLC shall notify Acme, Inc. if it determines that it can no longer meet the restrictions in this clause.
